title: Nodes No Ancestor Beats
statement:
You get the root of a binary tree. Call a node unbeaten if no node on the path from the root down to it (the root itself included) has a strictly larger value. A tie does not beat a node.

Return how many nodes are unbeaten. The root always is, since its path holds only itself.

Trees are written in level order with null for a missing child.

examples.why: 7, 9, 8 and 12 are unbeaten. 5 and 6 are each larger than their parent, but 7 sits above both of them. 8 is fine: the path 7 → 3 → 8 holds nothing above 8.
The three 4s all count, because an equal value does not beat a node. 2 and 1 are beaten by the root.
-5 and -2 count. Starting the running maximum at 0 instead of at the root's value would count nothing here.

constraints: The tree is at most 500 levels deep
hints: Whether a node counts depends only on the largest value above it. What would you need to carry down from the root to decide on the spot?
Walk the tree from the root and pass down the largest value seen on the path so far. Each node compares itself with that one number.
visit(node, maxAbove): count 1 if node.val ≥ maxAbove, then recurse into both children with max(maxAbove, node.val). Start with the root's own value as maxAbove.

explain.intuition:
A node is beaten if any ancestor is larger, and the only ancestor that matters is the largest one. So instead of looking back up the path at every node, carry the path's maximum down with you. Each node then makes its decision with one comparison, and hands its children the updated maximum.

This is the "pass state down" shape of tree problems, the mirror image of the "return a value up" shape used for heights. It is like a CSS property that inherits: each element sees what its ancestors set, and may override it for its own subtree. Two details decide correctness: ties count as unbeaten, so compare with ≥, and the starting maximum must be the root's value (or minus infinity), never 0, because values can be negative.
steps: Define visit(node, maxAbove) that returns how many unbeaten nodes are in this subtree.
Let here = node.val ≥ maxAbove ? 1 : 0 and m = max(maxAbove, node.val).
pitfalls: Comparing only with the parent. In the first example 5 beats its parent 3, but the root 7 still beats 5.
Using > instead of ≥. Equal values do not beat each other, so the second example would drop from 3 to 1.
Starting the maximum at 0. With all-negative values nothing would count, not even the root.

solutions.title: DFS carrying the path maximum
solutions.idea: Recurse from the root, passing down the largest value seen on the path. A node counts when it is at least that large.

solutions.title: Explicit stack of (node, path maximum)
solutions.idea: The same walk without recursion: every stack entry remembers the largest value on the path above it.

followups: Return the unbeaten values themselves, in level order.
Count nodes that are larger than every node below them instead. Which direction does the information now flow?
